descricao: How to describe any job in English — conditions, environment, feelings, and duties — in opposite pairs, plus the grammar and vocabulary that make professional descriptions sound natural.

secoes.conteudo:
'What do you do?' is one of the first questions strangers ask each other in English — at a party, on a flight, at a dinner table. It is asking: what is your job? And answering it naturally requires two things: vocabulary to name what you do, and vocabulary to describe what it is like.

At B1 level, you can already say 'I'm a teacher' or 'I work in finance.' But the conversation quickly goes further. Is it a good job? Is it **well-paid**? Do you enjoy it? What exactly does your work involve? This material gives you the vocabulary to answer all of those questions — and to understand them when you hear them.

You will learn job vocabulary in pairs: each quality opposite its contrast, each condition alongside what it looks like from the other side. By the end, you will be able to describe any job — yours or anyone else's — in fluent, natural English.

secoes.titulo: Hours and Pay: Full-Time / Part-Time, Well-Paid / Low-Paid
secoes.conteudo:
Let's start with the two most practical facts of any job: how many hours, and how much money.

**Full-time** and **part-time** describe how many hours a week a job requires. A **full-time** job typically means around 40 hours per week — the standard working schedule. A **part-time** job means fewer hours — perhaps 20, or even less. Part-time work is common for students, caregivers, and people balancing multiple responsibilities. 'I work full-time' and 'I work part-time' are very natural in everyday conversation.

**Well-paid** and **low-paid** describe the salary. A **well-paid** job offers good money for the work involved. A **low-paid** job offers relatively little. You might also hear **highly paid** as a stronger synonym for **well-paid**, and **badly paid** as an informal version of **low-paid**. The two core words to know are **salary** and **wages** — both refer to money you earn from work, but used slightly differently. **Salary** is a fixed monthly or annual amount, common in office and professional roles. **Wages** tend to refer to hourly or weekly pay, typically in manual or shift-based work.

Two more useful conditions: **flexible hours** means you can choose when you start and finish, within certain limits — a growing priority for many workers. **Shift work** means working in rotating blocks of time, including evenings or nights — common in healthcare, manufacturing, and hospitality. 'I work shifts' or 'I do shift work' signals a non-standard schedule.

Where and how a job happens shapes how it feels every day.

**Indoors** and **outdoors** describe the physical environment. An **indoors** job happens inside — in an office, a hospital, a school, a factory. An **outdoors** job happens outside — construction, agriculture, sports coaching, wildlife management. Many jobs are mixed: a salesperson might work from an office but spend significant time visiting clients. When someone describes a job as **outdoor work**, it usually implies physical activity and exposure to the weather — something some people love and others avoid.

The pair **independent** and **team-based** describes how you work with — or without — other people. An **independent** job lets you organize your own time and make your own decisions, with limited supervision. A **team-based** job means collaborating with colleagues, attending meetings, coordinating tasks, and communicating constantly. Neither is better; they suit different personalities. You might also hear **autonomous** as a synonym for **independent** — a word that appears often in job advertisements: 'We are looking for someone who can work autonomously.'

A third useful pair: **permanent** and **temporary**. A **permanent** position has no set end date — you are employed indefinitely, with job security. A **temporary** job is fixed to a specific period — a few months, a project, a season. 'I have a temporary contract' or 'it's a temp position' signals this. Temporary work is sometimes called **contract work** when it is project-based.

secoes.titulo: What It Feels Like: Rewarding / Tedious, Challenging / Routine
secoes.conteudo:
Beyond the practical facts, people describe their jobs in terms of how they feel to do every day. This is where the most revealing vocabulary lives.

**Rewarding** and **tedious** are the most important pair in this group. A **rewarding** job gives you a sense of meaning, satisfaction, or **fulfilment** — you feel that what you do matters, that it makes a real difference. Teaching, nursing, and social work are often described as **rewarding** because the impact on other people is visible and direct. Its opposite: **tedious**. A **tedious** job is repetitive, slow, and draining — the same tasks, over and over, without stimulation or variety. Every job has some **tedious** moments; a job that is mostly **tedious** is a different problem.

**Challenging** and **routine** describe the level of demand. A **challenging** job requires effort, problem-solving, and continuous learning — it pushes you, often in uncomfortable ways. Many people find this energizing. **Routine** describes a job with a predictable, repetitive structure — you do essentially the same things every day. Some people find this calming and reassuring; others find it stifling. Neither word is inherently negative — it depends entirely on what kind of work you want.

Two more useful adjectives: **stressful** means the job consistently produces pressure, anxiety, or a feeling of being overwhelmed. **Creative** means the work regularly involves generating new ideas, designing things, or finding original solutions. Both come up constantly when people talk about their professional lives.

secoes.titulo: What You Actually Do: Verbs for Job Duties
secoes.conteudo:
One of the most important things you can learn for talking about work is the vocabulary for describing job duties — the verbs that tell you what a person does in their role.

**Manage** means to be in charge of people or projects — organizing, overseeing, making decisions. 'She manages a team of twelve.' **Lead** is similar but with a stronger emphasis on direction and vision: 'He leads the product development team.' Both appear constantly in professional descriptions and on CVs.

**Deal with** means to handle something that requires attention — usually problems, people, or requests. 'She deals with customer complaints.' 'He deals with legal questions from clients.' It is one of the most flexible and useful phrases in professional English because it covers a huge range of activities without being overly specific.

**Report to** means to be accountable to a particular person or position. 'I report to the head of department.' 'She reports directly to the CEO.' This phrase appears constantly in job descriptions and organizational charts, describing the line of authority.

**Be responsible for** signals ownership of a task, area, or outcome — ongoing accountability, not just occasional action. 'He is responsible for quality control.' 'I am responsible for training all new staff.' It is more formal than 'deal with' and implies that something is genuinely yours to manage.

**Work with** means to collaborate regularly with a specific group. 'She works with clients from across Europe.' **Support** means to help someone or something function better: 'He supports the sales team.' 'The tool supports multiple languages.' **Develop** means to create and improve something over time — a product, a process, a team, a skill. **Coordinate** means to organize different elements so they work together smoothly.

secoes.titulo: Grammar: Simple Present for Professional Life
secoes.conteudo:
One of the most important uses of the simple present tense is for professional routines and ongoing facts — things that are true about your job in general, not just right now.

'She manages a team of eight people.' This is not happening at this specific moment — it is a standing, ongoing fact about her role.
'He deals with customer complaints every day.' A regular professional activity.
'I report to the head of department.' A permanent organizational relationship.
'We work with clients from different countries.' An ongoing professional reality.

This is the simple present used for professional facts and routines — stable truths about how someone's work life is structured. It is different from the present continuous ('She is managing a crisis right now'), which describes something happening at this specific moment.

The structure is exactly what you already know: subject + verb (with -s for third person singular) + object or complement. 'She manages.' 'He deals with.' 'I report to.' 'We work with.' At B1 level, the goal is not to learn the structure — you already know it. The goal is to use it confidently in professional contexts, because this is exactly how work descriptions sound in real English: calm, direct, and in the simple present.

One more pattern worth knowing: 'I am in charge of...' and 'I am responsible for...' These are not verbs in the same way, but they are extremely common and function identically in professional descriptions. 'I am in charge of the sales department' = 'I manage the sales department.' Two ways to say the same thing — both completely natural.

A few words in job vocabulary trap Portuguese speakers specifically — either because they look like something familiar, or because they work differently from what you might expect.

**Career** and **carrier**. These look nearly identical and mean very different things. A **career** is your carreira — your professional path over a lifetime. 'She has had an impressive career in medicine.' A **carrier** is something that transports or carries things — a mail carrier, an aircraft carrier. They are spelled differently (career with 'ea', carrier with 'ier'), but they are easy to confuse in writing.

**Profession**. In Portuguese, 'profissão' is a fairly general word for any job. In English, **profession** is slightly narrower: it tends to refer to skilled, often licensed occupations — medicine, law, architecture, teaching. For general jobs or occupations, **job**, **work**, or **occupation** are more natural in everyday conversation. 'What is your profession?' sounds formal or slightly limited. 'What do you do?' or 'What's your job?' is more natural in most situations.

**Office** and 'ofício'. An **office** is a place of work — a room or building where desk-based work happens. 'I work in an office.' In Portuguese, 'ofício' can mean a trade, a craft, or a formal official letter — none of which is what 'office' means in English. If someone says 'I'll drop it off at your office,' they mean your workplace, not a formal document.

**Currently**. This is worth mentioning because it pairs naturally with job descriptions: 'I'm currently working as a...' or 'She is currently managing...' Many Portuguese speakers reach for 'actually' here — which would mean 'na verdade' (a correction or emphasis). For 'currently' (meaning 'at this time, nowadays'), use **currently** or **at the moment**. 'I'm currently working in finance' = I am working in finance these days.
